column4: ch-002 (origin of the Sonni; our reading of Houdas's French)
column5: Our reading of Sa'di as translated by Houdas: the first Sonni, Ali-Kolon, and his brother Selman-Nar (sons of Za-Yasiboi) served the king of Mali, fled to Songhai and made themselves independent; Ali-Kolon took the title Sonni for freeing his people from Mali's yoke and Selman-Nar succeeded him. Sonni Ali, 'the great tyrant', is named as a much later king of the same dynasty whose son Abu Bakr Dao was displaced by Askia Muhammad. So the chronicle distinguishes Ali-Kolon, founder, from Sonni Ali of about 1464: Diop's 'Ali-Kolon, the future Sonni Ali' joins two men, while the young readers' glossary's Ali Koleni as a hostage who escaped is closer to the chronicle but its 1325 date is not given by Sa'di in this passage. This is our own reading of the French, not a published translation of these lines; Houdas's notes also doubt the Yemeni origin of the Dia. Quote nothing.

column4: ch-003 (Kankan-Mousa in the Tarikh es-Soudan; our reading of Houdas's French)
column5: Our reading: Sa'di (writing in the 1650s) says Kankan-Mousa was the first Mali king to take Songhai, a pious and just ruler who made the pilgrimage in the early 9th century of the Hijra (Houdas's note gives 724 AH, 1324, after Ibn Khaldun), with a cortege of sixty thousand and five hundred slaves each carrying a gold rod of 500 mithqals; he adds that eastern annals did not call him generous, because his alms in the two holy cities were only 20,000 gold pieces against 100,000 from Askia Muhammad. So the sixty-thousand and gold-staff figures in the young readers' book, and the 20,000 and 100,000 comparison in Diop, come from Sa'di's chronicle, a 17th-century Timbuktu source about events 330 years earlier, not from the 14th-century Cairo witnesses. Sa'di also says Musa built a mosque outside Gao and the royal palace at Timbuktu, 'it is said' built the Timbuktu minaret, that a Mossi king sacked Timbuktu and Akil of the Tuareg held it forty years, and he quotes Ibn Battuta on a Cairo loan from Siraj al-Din. Use for Module 4 lesson 2: name the source of the numbers (Sa'di, late and distant) and keep them [CONTESTED]. Our own reading of French; quote nothing.

column4: ch-004 (the kingdom of Mali; our reading of Houdas's French)
column5: Our reading: Sa'di's description of Mali has a king served by a chamberlain-like official (Fala-Faran) who spoke for twelve district chiefs in each of three principalities (Kala, Bindougou, Sibridougou), two generals (Sanqar-Zouma for the south, Faran-Sura for the north), conquests of Songhai, Timbuktu, Zagha, Mima and Baghena, and a story that Mali's power ended after a miraculous massacre and then split into three; Jenne is said to have beaten Mali ninety-nine times. He also repeats a tradition of 44 white kings of Ghana, 22 before and 22 after the Hijra, which Houdas's notes treat with caution. A native-written, but late, outline of Mali's administration; it adds district chiefs and generals to the young readers' bureaucracy line, and the 44-king list is [TRADITIONAL DATE]. Quote nothing.

column4: ch-007 (Timbuktu's founding and rulers; our reading of Houdas's French)
column5: Our reading: Sa'di says Timbuktu was founded by Tuareg (Maghcharen) at the end of the 5th century AH (about 1100 CE) as a summer camp and store, named from a slave woman, 'the old woman', who guarded their goods; it first overshadowed the older market town Biro (Walata), its civilisation (religion and trade) came 'only from the Maghreb', houses went from thorn enclosures and straw huts to clay huts and a low wall, then a great mosque and later the mosque of Sankore, and the town only filled out by the mid 10th century AH under Askia Daoud. He gives rule by Mali for a century from 737 AH (1336-7), Tuareg for forty years from 837 AH (1433-4), Sonni Ali from 873 AH (1468-9) for twenty-four years, the askias from 14 Jumada II 898 AH (02/04/1493) to 12/04/1591, then the Moroccans; a hereditary governor, the Tombouctou-Koy, kept a third of the taxes. This is the Timbuktu native chronicle's own origin story, written by a proud Timbuktu notable in the 1650s: it supports the course's cautious wording that Sankore grew as a set of mosques and that Mansa Musa did not found a university (the course should not say Musa built Sankore), but its 'founded about 1100' is tradition [TRADITIONAL DATE] and its Mali date 1336 conflicts with Musa's 1324-25 pilgrimage reading only if read as a rule start. Quote nothing.

column4: ch-010 chunk 1 (Sonni Ali in Sa'di; our reading of Houdas's French)
column5: Our reading: Sa'di calls Sonni Ali a tyrant and persecutor of Timbuktu's scholars and gives dates: reign began 869 AH (1464-5) on an outside witness (al-Alqami), lasted 27 or 28 years; he took Jenne after holding it a year and a month, entered Timbuktu on 4 or 5 Rajab 873 AH (about 29-30 January 1468) and ruined it, killed or humiliated scholars (flight of Sankore's jurists to Biro with a thousand camels, a massacre of thirty girls, executions at Tadjit and Alfa'a-Konko) until 875 AH, yet also said that without scholars there would be no pleasure in the world, and cheated on his daily prayers; his Askia Muhammad often disobeyed his killing orders; Sonni Ali dug a canal toward Biro and was stopped by a Mossi march in 1480. This is the hostile portrait Diop reads as self-defence of the native religion; Sa'di's own bias (a Timbuktu scholar's family, Ahmad Baba cited) is plain. Module 4 lesson 3 should present Sa'di's Sonni Ali as one interested source [CONTESTED]. Quote nothing.

column4: ch-010 chunk 2 (Sonni Ali's death; our reading of Houdas's French)
column5: Our reading: Sa'di dates Sonni Ali's victory over the Mossi to 888 AH (1483), the arrest of the Timbuktu governor in 891 AH (1486), his death on 15 Muharram 898 AH (6 November 1492) on return from Gourma, drowned in a torrent, with his body filled with honey; the chronicler adds that this was God's punishment for tyranny. The death date (1492) and the course's Sonni Ali c. 1464 start agree with this chronicle; the moralising frame is Sa'di's. Quote nothing.

column4: ch-011 chunk 1 (Askia Muhammad's rise and pilgrimage; our reading of Houdas's French)
column5: Our reading: Askia Muhammad, a general of Sonni Ali, attacked Sonni Ali's son Abu Bakr Dao and won on 14 Jumada I 898 AH (3 March 1493), the son fled to Abar; the nickname Askia comes from the daughters' cry 'he is not' (said to mean 'he is not [the ruler]'); he separated army and people, rewarded the Timbuktu notables, left on the pilgrimage in Safar 902 AH (October 1495) with 1,500 men and 300,000 gold pieces taken from Sonni Ali's treasury, gave 100,000 to the two holy cities and bought a garden in Medina, was appointed lieutenant by the Abbasid caliph in Cairo, returned in 1497, then waged declared jihad on the Mossi and conquered Mali's old provinces; Sa'di also says the Songhai army 'delivered' itself of the Zabirbenda by sending them to die at Berko in about 1504. Reader and the Hakluyt editor's notes agree on the 300,000 figure for the pilgrimage fund. This gives a dated, native-written Askia pilgrimage beside Musa's: the 100,000 gold pieces of alms is what the Musa comparison (20,000) rests on. Sa'di is again a Timbuktu notable with a Sunni Maliki view and a bias toward the dynasty that favoured Timbuktu [CONTESTED]. Our own reading of the French; quote nothing.

column4: ch-011 chunk 2 (Askia Muhammad's reign and fall; our reading of Houdas's French)
column5: Our reading: campaigns include Katsena (1513), Agadez (1514-15), a Konta revolt that stayed independent; his son Mousa, jealous of the chamberlain Ali-Folen and of a favoured relative, overthrew the blind old Askia on 26 August 1528 (a feast day) after a succession quarrel; the chronicler says he reigned thirty-six years and six months. Sa'di's succession and family-intrigue detail confirms that Songhai succession was by competition within one family (as Diop's summary says) and gives an inside-court account of the 1528 coup; the chronicle's dates are given in Hijri with our conversions. Quote nothing.
